summary: A 1975 working paper on how to keep duplicated copies of a database consistent across a network. It discusses the general problem, then gives a detailed solution for one kind of duplicate database. The ideas were used for the TIP user identification database.

eli5.summary: Keeping the same list on many computers is hard when someone changes it. This note shows a way to keep every copy matching.

subtitle: How to keep duplicate copies of a database consistent across a network despite delays and failures

tldr.problem: Keeping identical copies of a database on multiple computers is impossible when communication between them has delays. Deciding which version is authoritative when updates arrive out of order becomes complex.
tldr.mechanism: Use timestamps to mark each modification and each entry's creation, along with a DBMP (Database Management Process) identifier to break ties. When updates arrive out of order, keep the one with the most recent timestamp. Mark deleted entries instead of removing them immediately, allowing late updates to be properly ordered.
tldr.outcome: The system guarantees eventual consistency: once updates stop and all copies receive all changes, the databases become identical. This approach was used for the TIP user identification database and provides a model for distributed database problems.

facts.label: Tuple size
facts.value: 5 components: selector, value, deleted flag, creation timestamp, modification timestamp

facts.label: Entry state
facts.value: Marked for deletion rather than removed

today: RFC 677 presents principles that influenced modern distributed database systems, particularly in handling eventual consistency and conflict resolution through vector clocks and versions. Systems like distributed NoSQL databases and version control systems use similar concepts to manage replicated data.

sections.title: The Distributed Database Problem
sections.content:
RFC 677 tackles the problem of keeping identical copies of a database on multiple computers in a network. Two key motivations drive this need: reliability (redundant copies survive individual system failures) and efficiency (copies kept near users serve them faster).

The challenge is that network communication has delay, and computers can crash or lose connectivity. When one database management process (DBMP) modifies an entry, other DBMPs may receive the change at different times, in different orders, and may be temporarily isolated from each other. The system must guarantee that all copies eventually become identical despite these obstacles.
sections.eli5: You want to keep the same list on many computers so it is reliable and fast. But when one computer changes it, the others find out at different times.

sections.title: Timestamps and Consistency
sections.content:
The RFC models a database as a collection of (selector, value) pairs, where the selector is a unique key. Four operations are allowed: selection (retrieve a value), assignment (change a value), creation (add a new entry), and deletion (remove an entry).

The core innovation is the use of timestamps to determine which update is authoritative. Each modification is tagged with a pair (time, dbmp-id), where time is the modification time and dbmp-id identifies which database process originated the change. When two DBMPs have assigned different values to the same entry, the one with the more recent timestamp wins. To handle ties, the DBMP identifiers are ordered, so (T1, D1) > (T2, D2) if T1 > T2, or if times are equal and D1 > D2.

Each entry in the database becomes a 5-tuple: (selector, value, deleted-flag, creation-timestamp, modification-timestamp). The timestamps allow a DBMP to correctly order received updates, even if they arrive out of order.
sections.eli5: Every change gets a timestamp saying when it happened and where it came from. If two computers change the same thing, whoever changed it more recently wins.

sections.title: Handling Creation and Deletion
sections.content:
Creation of new entries is straightforward: a DBMP creates a new entry and sends it to all others. But deletion poses a problem. If a DBMP deletes an entry locally and another DBMP assigns a new value to it before hearing about the deletion, the value update might recreate the entry at a third DBMP that heard the assignment before the deletion.

The solution: instead of immediately removing deleted entries, mark them with a deleted flag. A marked entry persists in the database. When an assignment arrives for a deleted entry, the system compares creation timestamps: the creation timestamp of the incoming assignment versus the creation timestamp of the deleted entry. The entry with the later creation time is kept. This way, assignments to a truly deleted entry (with an old creation timestamp) are ignored, but assignments to a recreated entry (with a new creation timestamp) are accepted.

The modification tuple encodes the operation type implicitly: creation is marked by creation-timestamp = modification-timestamp, assignment by creation-timestamp < modification-timestamp, and deletion by the deleted flag being set. There is no need to separately communicate "what type of operation this is."
sections.eli5: Instead of erasing an entry, mark it as deleted. This way, if someone changes it before hearing it was deleted, you can figure out what really happened.

sections.title: Eventual Consistency and Garbage Collection
sections.content:
The system guarantees eventual consistency: given a cessation of updates to any entry, and sufficient time for all DBMPs to communicate with all others, the entry's state (existence and value) will be identical in all copies. This is a weaker guarantee than total consistency at all times, but necessary in a network with delays.

A practical limitation is that deleted entries are never automatically removed (only marked); they accumulate as "garbage." The RFC discusses the possibility of garbage collection: periodically removing marked entries after confirming that all other DBMPs have received and processed the deletion and no new assignments are arriving for them.

The design assumes messages between DBMPs are delivered in the same order they are sent, which holds for the ARPANET. For networks without this guarantee, ordering protocols would be added above this mechanism.
sections.eli5: Eventually, every computer catches up and has the same data. Old deleted entries could be cleaned up later, but the system doesn't do it automatically.
